Finance Betting games · the coin flip

Betting everything makes the average rich and almost every player poor

A thousand players bet a hundred times on a fair coin: +50% on heads, −40% on tails. The average round adds 5%, yet staking everything leaves the typical player with half a penny on the pound. A smaller stake, or shared luck, turns the same coin into growth.

Quick build: fewer trials, so the ranks in stage 2 are noisy. Rebuild without --quick for the real figures.
1 · All in

Everyone stakes all they have, every round.

The average climbs while the typical player sinks

2 · One Kelly player

A 1001st player stakes a quarter each round, on coins of their own.

Kelly's rule picks the stake that grows wealth fastest over many rounds, by maximising the expected log of wealth. For a bet that gains b with probability p and loses a otherwise, f* = p / a − (1 − p) / b.

3 · Everyone sensible

Each player bets on their own coin, at Kelly or all in, alone or pooled.

4 · A mixed table

A quarter of each: all in, pooled; Kelly, pooled; all in, alone; Kelly, alone.

Two levers

Pooling changes the bet; Kelly sizes the stake on it.

Two levers: the bet you hold, and how much you stake

The bet: one coin, or the pool's average

The stake: set by Kelly

What Kelly does not promise

Fair play

Every stake is set before the flip, from the bet's public terms and what that player has seen. Outcomes are drawn in advance only so that every scheme faces the same luck. Tested: two tables that agree on everything a player has seen give that player the same stakes.
